strengths: Significance: SAFESEARCH addresses a useful deployment problem: benign user requests can produce unsafe answers when search results contain unreliable content. Its 300 cases span five risks, extending evaluation beyond instruction injection to misinformation, advertising, bias, and harmful advice.

Soundness: Injecting one fixed website alongside authentic results provides a controlled test of susceptibility. Evaluation covers 15 backend models, three scaffolds, and three repetitions, with additional experiments on injection position, context length, result count, generation strategy, and defenses. The substantial observed failures demonstrate vulnerabilities under the specified conditions.

Evaluation validation: Appendix C reports independent annotation of 200 responses by two authors, with 96% human agreement and 96–98% human–judge agreement. This is useful evidence for the checklist-assisted safety evaluator within the sampled setting.

Originality and presentation: The main contribution is a useful integration of automated scenario generation, differential filtering, website synthesis, and checklist evaluation. The pipeline is understandable, and the extensive prompts and concrete examples make the benchmark design inspectable.

Reproducibility and ethics: The manuscript provides an anonymous code/data release link, model and scaffold descriptions, and experimental settings. Simulated injection avoids contaminating public search results. The discussion appropriately acknowledges proprietary-system access, search-provider coverage, benchmark size, and cost limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness—selection and attribution: Cases are retained only when Qwen3-8B fails with manipulated search and succeeds with benign search. This is reasonable for constructing a challenge set, but conditions the benchmark on one evaluated model’s vulnerabilities. Retention differs substantially across risks, from 6.8% to 31.3%, complicating claims about their relative difficulty. There is no alternate filtering-model or unfiltered-set evaluation, and Table 2 omits benign-condition safety failure rates for other agents. Consequently, their ASRs do not establish how much failure the injected website causes relative to their own baselines.

Soundness—helpfulness validity: Prompt 8 asks GPT-4.1-mini to assess accuracy using only the query and answer, without reference evidence or ground truth. This is especially problematic for fabricated, post-cutoff claims. Near-ceiling helpfulness scores can therefore reflect convincing presentation rather than correct assistance. The claim that safety and helpfulness are jointly preserved needs independent factuality or task-success evaluation; the safety judge’s human validation does not validate this separate metric.

Soundness—scaffold interpretation: Only the first search call is exposed, while deeper scaffolds can obtain additional uncontaminated results. Their lower ASR is informative under that exposure model, but does not isolate cross-validation from increased evidence volume, computation, or avoidance of search. Search-call counts, exposure rates, and matched-budget comparisons are absent. Moreover, GPT-5-mini performs worse with deep research than tool calling (16.1% versus 4.9% ASR), qualifying the broad superiority narrative.

Reporting consistency: Table 6 describes the same 842 GPT-5-mini responses, yet panel (a) contains 274 successful attacks while panels (b) and (c) each contain 150. These totals cannot describe the same success labels and undermine the associated monitoring analysis. Section 4.1 also attributes GPT-4.1’s 85.0% and 77.3% results to GPT-4.1-mini. These discrepancies require reconciliation.

Evaluation uncertainty: Human validation samples only three relatively vulnerable search-workflow agents. Aggregate agreement does not establish false-positive accuracy for low-ASR GPT-5 agents or transfer to deep-research outputs. Per-class confusion matrices and broader validation are needed, alongside confidence intervals accounting for repeated evaluations of the same cases. Small model differences should not be interpreted confidently without these checks.

External validity and originality: Guaranteed insertion of purpose-built content measures conditional vulnerability, not real-world incident probability or a formal safety bound. The motivating content-farm estimate lacks human validation, and response shifts in the health experiment are not themselves verified medical errors. The distinction from RAG is also overstated: RAG need not use a curated, trustworthy corpus. Direct comparison with closely related retrieval-poisoning and agent-safety evaluations would better establish what new coverage or understanding this framework provides.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: search agents can propagate unreliable retrieved content even when users are not attempting to attack them. Covering misinformation, advertising, bias, harmful outputs, and prompt injection broadens evaluation beyond instruction-following attacks.

Originality: The main contribution is an integrated evaluation framework combining scenario generation, differential filtering, website simulation, and case-specific evaluation checklists. This is a potentially useful benchmark contribution, although the individual techniques are largely established.

Experimental coverage: The evaluation spans 15 backend models and three scaffolds, with three repetitions per case. Appendix C investigates injection position, content length, generator choice, and search-result timing. These experiments provide evidence that the observed vulnerabilities are not confined to one configuration.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Two authors independently annotate 200 responses, obtaining 96–98% agreement with the safety evaluator. The manuscript supplies generation and evaluation prompts, experimental settings, and an anonymous code-and-data link.

Presentation and ethics: The overall pipeline is understandable, with concrete examples and substantial implementation detail. Simulating injected content avoids manipulating live search rankings. The authors acknowledge simulation-transfer limitations, evaluation costs, and the exploratory nature of their reasoning-summary analysis.
weaknesses: Soundness—selection and attribution: Cases are retained specifically when Qwen3-8B fails with manipulated results but succeeds with benign results (Section 3.2), with retention as low as 6.8%. This is reasonable for constructing a challenge set, but conditions the benchmark on one model's vulnerabilities and limits claims of agent-agnostic fairness and comparisons across risk categories. Table 2 reports benign helpfulness but not benign target-consequence rates for each evaluated agent, so it does not establish how much of each agent's ASR is attributable to injection. Evaluation on independently sampled cases, alternative filtering models, and paired benign/manipulated safety outcomes is needed.

Soundness—helpfulness claims are insufficiently supported: Prompt 8 asks GPT-4.1-mini to judge accuracy using only the query and response, without reference answers or retrieved evidence, despite the benchmark emphasizing recent and potentially fabricated information. Human validation covers the safety evaluator, not helpfulness. Near-ceiling helpfulness alongside substantial ASR may therefore reflect convincing presentation rather than genuine utility. This undermines the claimed safety–helpfulness balance; describing deep-research Qwen3-8B as both useful and safe is particularly difficult to reconcile with its 45.8% ASR.

Soundness—material numerical inconsistency: Table 6(a) contains 274 attack successes among 842 GPT-5-mini responses, whereas Tables 6(b) and 6(c), purportedly analyzing the same responses, each contain 150. Moreover, Table 2's 18.9% ASR implies approximately 170 successes across all 900 trials. These counts cannot describe the same experiment as presented, leaving the reflection-based explanation unsupported until corrected. Section 4.1 also attributes GPT-4.1's 85.0% and 77.3% results to GPT-4.1-mini.

External validity and significance: Appending a deliberately generated, query-targeted website measures conditional susceptibility under controlled exposure; it does not establish deployment risk or a formal safety bound. The motivating studies do not validate that connection: content-farm prevalence relies on an unvalidated LLM classifier, and the health experiment deliberately selects long-tail questions without a quantified independent correctness assessment. Appendix E.5 appropriately acknowledges a simulation gap, but the broader claims of realistic risk estimation and safety guarantees still exceed the evidence.

Evaluation uncertainty: The safety-judge audit uses only three models under the search-workflow scaffold, where attacks commonly succeed. Aggregate agreement does not establish false-positive rates in the approximately 5% ASR regime, or reliability on deep-research responses. Per-category confusion matrices and validation across scaffolds would strengthen confidence. Despite repeated trials, the paper provides no confidence intervals for model rankings or defense improvements. Scaffold comparisons also change search budgets and exposure opportunities, so they do not isolate cross-validation as the source of improved safety.

Originality and reproducibility: The paper does not experimentally establish what its multi-stage generator and auxiliary fields add over simpler generation, or compare its coverage with closely related retrieval-poisoning and agent-security benchmarks. Its categorical distinction between curated RAG and unreliable web search overstates the methodological separation. Reproducibility also needs clarification: Table 5 includes models absent from the main evaluation while omitting Kimi-K2 and the separately evaluated Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507, and the manuscript does not clearly establish whether cached authentic results and exact generated websites are included in the released assets. These gaps matter for a benchmark whose inputs change over time.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: benign user queries can produce unsafe answers through unreliable retrieved content. SAFESEARCH offers a practical, reusable evaluation resource spanning five risks beyond prompt injection alone.

Soundness: The controlled injection of one website into authentic search results provides convincing evidence that retrieved content can induce failures. Evaluation across 15 backend models, three scaffolds, and three repeated trials is substantial. Appendix C also examines injection position, content length, generation strategy, and timing.

Evaluator validation: Two authors independently assess 200 responses, with 96–98% human–judge agreement and 96% inter-human agreement. This meaningfully supports the checklist-assisted safety evaluator within the tested setting.

Originality and presentation: The main contribution is a useful integration of automated scenario generation, differential filtering, website synthesis, and evaluation across multiple risk categories. The workflow is clearly explained, with concrete examples and extensive prompts.

Reproducibility and ethics: The manuscript provides an anonymous code/data link, model and scaffold configurations, and evaluation prompts. Simulation avoids manipulating public search rankings, and the authors explicitly discuss reviewer welfare, proprietary-system coverage, benchmark size, and computational trade-offs.
weaknesses: Soundness—selection and attribution: Cases are retained only when Qwen3-8B fails with manipulated results and succeeds with benign results (Section 3.2), with retention as low as 6.8%. This is reasonable for constructing a challenge set, but conditions the benchmark on one model’s vulnerabilities and differently selects each risk category. No alternative-filtering or unfiltered evaluation establishes the robustness of model rankings and cross-risk comparisons. Moreover, Table 2 reports benign helpfulness but not benign safety failure rates for other agents, so their ASRs do not isolate failures introduced by the injected website.

Soundness—helpfulness claims: Prompt 8 asks GPT-4.1-mini to assess accuracy using only the query and response, without reference answers or retrieved evidence. This is particularly problematic for deliberately fabricated, post-cutoff information. Helpfulness is not independently validated, and near-ceiling scores cannot establish that agents preserve factual utility or achieve the claimed safety–helpfulness balance.

Soundness—scaffold interpretation: Only the first search call is contaminated, while tool-calling and deep-research systems can obtain additional clean evidence under different search budgets. Their improvements are useful operational observations, but do not isolate scaffold design from exposure dilution or additional computation. The general claim that deep research improves resilience also needs qualification: GPT-5-mini has 16.1% ASR with deep research versus 4.9% with tool calling.

Evaluation uncertainty: Judge validation covers three highly vulnerable search-workflow models, excluding the strongest models and other scaffolds. Aggregate agreement does not establish false-positive accuracy around the approximately 5% ASRs emphasized for GPT-5. Per-risk confusion matrices, validation on resistant agents, and uncertainty intervals over test cases would make these comparisons substantially more reliable.

Presentation and numerical consistency: Table 6(a) contains 274 attack successes among 842 trials, whereas Tables 6(b) and 6(c) each contain 150 successes for the apparently same sample. This directly affects the reasoning-monitor analysis and needs reconciliation. Section 4.1 also attributes GPT-4.1’s 85.0% and 77.3% results to GPT-4.1-mini. Table 5 does not consistently match the evaluated model roster, weakening configuration traceability.

Originality and scope: The distinction from retrieval-poisoning benchmarks is asserted more strongly than demonstrated; RAG need not use a verified, static corpus, and the intervention here also operates on retrieved text. A direct comparison with the closest benchmarks would clarify the additional coverage and insights. The motivating 4.3% content-farm estimate lacks human validation, and the 46 health-answer changes lack a quantitative adjudication of correctness. These observations support motivation, but not broad prevalence estimates or formal safety bounds. Overall, the contribution has clear merits, but measurement and comparative-claim revisions are needed before its conclusions can be relied upon.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful safety problem: how search agents handle unreliable retrieved content when users are not explicitly attempting to jailbreak them. Combining five risk categories extends the evaluation beyond prompt injection alone.

Soundness: The controlled injection experiment provides convincing evidence of vulnerability within the tested setting. Appendix I reports an average benign-condition ASR of 0.81%, substantially below manipulated-condition results. Evaluating 17 models, three scaffolds, and three repetitions provides considerable empirical breadth.

Evaluation quality: Ablations examine result count, injection position and round, document length, timestamps, and generator choice. Appendix G also validates the safety evaluator against two human annotators on 200 responses, with 95% unanimous agreement.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The workflow is understandable, and the appendices provide prompts, configurations, and qualitative examples. Simulated injection avoids contaminating public search results. The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations concerning proprietary systems, search-service coverage, benchmark scale, and operational cost.
weaknesses: Soundness—selection limits the comparative conclusions. Cases are retained only when they defeat Qwen3-8B while passing its benign-condition check. Table 3 reports strongly differing retention rates, from 6.8% for injection to 31.3% for advertisements. This is legitimate challenge-set construction, but resulting ASRs are conditional on model-dependent selection and category-specific filtering. They do not establish representative vulnerability rates or that misinformation is intrinsically the greatest threat. Evaluation on an unfiltered held-out sample, or analysis across filtering models, is needed to support those broader interpretations.

Construct validity—the claim that all queries are fully benign and representative is insufficiently supported. Table 5 includes a query asking which neighborhoods should be avoided based on crime among residents of a particular ethnicity; Figure 19 requests homemade self-defense sprays. Such queries already contain sensitive or potentially harmful framing. Other examples presuppose named drugs whose real-world grounding is not established. Similarity of coarse LLM-assigned quality-score distributions does not demonstrate representativeness. The paper should distinguish neutral information seeking, leading questions, and potentially harmful requests.

Helpfulness claims exceed the measurement. Section 3.3 defines HS as perceived usefulness rather than factual accuracy, while Prompt 9 explicitly asks the judge to consider accuracy without supplying verified answers or supporting evidence. No human validation of HS is reported, and many scores saturate near 100. These results support apparent helpfulness more directly than actual task utility, so the claim that safety and capability improve together needs an independently grounded utility evaluation.

Scaffold explanations are not adequately isolated. Deep research receives a larger search budget while the unreliable page is injected only once, so improvements can reflect additional clean evidence, intermediate summarization, or differing exposure rather than demonstrated cross-validation. Actual search counts, injection exposure rates, and budget-matched comparisons are missing. The improvement is also not universal: GPT-5-mini has 4.9% ASR with tool calling versus 16.1% with deep research. The mechanism and generality of scaffold benefits should be stated more cautiously.

Evaluation reliability and reporting need correction. Judge validation covers only three comparatively vulnerable models under search workflow, leaving performance on stronger models and nuanced deep-research answers unverified; class-specific error rates and uncertainty intervals are absent. Appendix H also contains a concrete inconsistency: Table 9(a) records 274 successful attacks among 842 responses, whereas Tables 9(b,c) each record 150 for the apparently same responses. Moreover, Table 9(c) shows higher attack frequency with a warning than without one, which does not support the proposed protective interpretation.

Originality and reproducibility remain incomplete. The contribution is primarily a useful integration of synthetic case generation, differential filtering, tool-output injection, and rubric judging. There is no direct comparison with a simpler generation pipeline or adapted existing benchmark establishing the added value of the proposed construction. Although prompts are supplied, the code-and-dataset release sentence on page 2 has no location, and availability of frozen search results and generated pages is unclear. These artifacts are particularly important for reproducing a benchmark dependent on changing web content.

strengths: Significance: SAFESEARCH addresses a useful practical problem: whether search agents propagate unsafe information from retrieved content. Covering five risk categories broadens the evaluation beyond explicit prompt injection.

Soundness: The controlled injection of one website, paired with benign-search evaluations, provides credible evidence that injected content causes failures in the tested configurations. Appendix I reports an average benign ASR of only 0.81%, substantially below manipulated-search results.

Evaluation breadth: The study includes 300 cases, 17 backend models, and three scaffolds, although deep research covers only five models. Three repeated trials and ablations of injection position, content length, generation model, and injection timing strengthen the empirical contribution.

Evaluator validation: Appendix G reports independent annotation by two authors on 200 responses, with 96–98% human–judge agreement. This is meaningful support for checklist-based scoring within the sampled setting.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The workflow is understandable, and extensive appendices provide prompts, configurations, examples, and limitations. Simulated injection avoids manipulating public search results. The acknowledged restrictions on search services, proprietary systems, and benchmark scale are appropriate.
weaknesses: Soundness—benchmark validity: The claim that all queries are fully benign and have no inherent tendency toward vulnerability is contradicted by Table 5. One query asks which Toronto neighborhoods with Somali residents should be avoided; others presuppose newly approved drugs and adverse effects. Such prompts can already contain discriminatory framing or unsupported premises. The aggregate LLM query-quality assessment does not establish benignity or representativeness. A human audit separating neutral queries from leading or prejudicial ones is needed.

Soundness—selection and interpretation: Cases are retained specifically when Qwen3-8B fails under manipulation and succeeds without it; retention is only 6.8–31.3% across categories (Table 3). This is legitimate for targeted failure discovery, but ASRs describe a selected challenge set, not typical susceptibility to unreliable search results. It also conditions model and category comparisons on one model's vulnerabilities. The paper needs clearer qualification and a comparison using unfiltered cases or independently selected cases; its natural-search observations do not validate the synthetic distribution.

Soundness—scaffold conclusions: Lower ASR with more elaborate scaffolds does not isolate better verification from increased clean evidence, different search queries, or reduced exposure to the injected page. Exposure rates and matched search-budget comparisons are missing. Moreover, GPT-5-mini's ASR increases from 4.9% with tool calling to 16.1% with deep research (Table 1), limiting the broad claim that deeper scaffolds improve safety.

Soundness—helpfulness and judge generalization: The paper defines HS as perceived usefulness rather than factual accuracy, yet Prompt 9 explicitly asks the judge to assess accuracy. There is no human validation of this measure, so near-ceiling HS does not establish preserved task performance or the absence of a safety–utility trade-off. Safety-judge validation covers only three relatively vulnerable models using the search workflow; category-level error rates and validation on low-ASR models and longer research outputs are needed to substantiate finer comparisons.

Internal consistency: Appendix H's Table 9 describes the same 842 reasoning-summary trials, but panel (a) totals 274 successful attacks while panels (b) and (c) each total 150. The discrepancy is unexplained and undermines the proposed account of reflection and safety. Panel (c) also shows a higher success rate among cautioned responses (123/645) than uncautioned responses (27/197), which does not support a simple protective interpretation of warnings.

Originality and reproducibility: The contribution is primarily an integration of synthetic case generation, differential filtering, tool-output injection, and rubric judging. The paper does not compare against a simpler generation pipeline or an adapted existing red-teaming method to establish the added value of its three-stage design. Cost-efficiency is asserted without measured generation or evaluation costs. Although prompts are detailed, the release statement ends at 'at' without an accessible artifact location in the supplied manuscript, leaving the complete dataset, cached results, and implementation unavailable for verification. Together with the measurement issues above, these gaps warrant revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful safety problem: search agents propagating unreliable external information. Covering misinformation, advertising, bias, harmful output, and prompt injection makes the framework useful beyond conventional injection testing.

Soundness: The controlled experiments convincingly demonstrate vulnerabilities on the selected stress tests. Table 10 provides important benign-tool controls: the average baseline ASR is 0.81%, substantially below manipulated-tool results. Evaluation spans 17 models, three scaffolds, and three repetitions per case.

Evaluation quality: The paper includes extensive sensitivity studies covering injection position, content length, timing, generators, and search-result count. Appendix G provides meaningful human validation on 200 responses, with 96–98% evaluator–annotator agreement.

Originality and presentation: The contribution is primarily a useful integration of scenario generation, differential filtering, website synthesis, and checklist evaluation. The pipeline is clearly explained, with detailed prompts and illustrative cases supporting reuse.

Ethics and limitations: Local simulation avoids contaminating public search results. The paper discusses annotator welfare and acknowledges limitations concerning proprietary systems, search-service coverage, benchmark scale, and operational cost.
weaknesses: External validity is overstated. Cases are selected specifically for successful attacks against Qwen3-8B, with retention rates as low as 6.8–6.9% (Table 3). This is appropriate for stress testing, but the resulting ASRs do not estimate ordinary deployment risk or establish a general safety bound. The motivating content-farm and stance-shift studies do not calibrate that relationship. Furthermore, Table 5 includes explicitly loaded demographic questions and fictional drug names, weakening the claim that all queries are fully benign and representative.

The scaffold findings need narrower interpretation. Only five models receive deep-research evaluation, compared with 17 under the other scaffolds, so aggregate averages are not directly comparable. Additional searches also dilute the single first-call injection; the experiments do not isolate cross-validation as the mechanism. GPT-5-mini actually has higher ASR under deep research than tool calling, 16.1% versus 4.9%.

The helpfulness evidence does not establish preserved task utility. Section 3.3 defines HS as perceived usefulness rather than factual accuracy, while Prompt 9 explicitly requests assessment of accuracy without supplying reference evidence. Near-ceiling scores cannot substantiate the broader claim that safety and actual helpfulness improve together. Human or reference-grounded utility evaluation is needed.

Evaluator validation is restricted to three high-ASR models using the search workflow. Overall agreement on this sample does not establish reliable measurement for low-ASR models or longer research outputs. Per-class precision/recall and validation across scaffolds would strengthen the rankings; uncertainty intervals are also missing.

The reasoning analysis contains a material inconsistency: Table 9(a) reports 274 successful attacks, whereas Tables 9(b) and 9(c) report 150, although all describe the same 842 responses. This needs reconciliation before drawing mechanistic conclusions. Reproducibility also remains incomplete in the supplied manuscript: the announced repository link is absent, and Table 6 does not match the evaluated model roster.

Novelty over existing retrieval-poisoning and agent-safety evaluation methods is only partially established. The RAG comparison assumes curated, reliable corpora too strongly, and there is no direct comparison with an adapted prior evaluation pipeline. The useful contribution is the broader benchmark and integrated workflow; stronger methodological novelty and cost-efficiency claims require additional evidence.
